language.script_notes: Lao is a rounded abugida related to Thai but visibly simpler — fewer characters, more curves, and none of Thai's tall vertical 'flags'. It is clearly not Khmer (which is angular and dense) or Burmese (circular). Sample shown is the stop-sign word ຢຸດ; verify a longer sample against real signage. .la domain.

road_furniture.bollard_shape: Angular post, close to the Thai design.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Minimal; many rural and mountain roads have no barrier at all.
road_furniture.line_paint: Frequently unmarked; a centre line where roads are properly paved. The back of some road signs is light blue.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Distinctive segmented, tapering concrete 'pinecone' utility poles are a signature Laos tell. Concrete kilometre posts on the main routes.

architecture.roof_style: Steep, multi-tiered, overlapping temple (wat) roofs; simple gables on houses.
architecture.roof_material: Corrugated metal, some clay tile, thatch in villages.
architecture.wall_construction: Wooden stilt houses in the countryside; brick and render in towns; French colonial shophouses with shutters and teak balconies in Vientiane and Luang Prabang.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Bare weathered timber, whitewash, faded colour; gilded and mirror-mosaic temple exteriors.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Wooden stilt houses; gilded Buddhist wats with steep layered roofs; the golden Pha That Luang stupa; well-preserved French colonial streets in Luang Prabang.

nature.vegetation: Dense tropical monsoon forest, teak, and bamboo; rice on the Mekong lowlands; visible slash-and-burn clearings on hillsides.
nature.terrain: Very mountainous, especially in the north; the Mekong River forms much of the western border with Thailand, and most towns sit on flat river land with hills always visible around them.
nature.climate_signature: Tropical monsoon, hot. Skies are often thick with haze and smoke during the March–April agricultural burning season.

vehicles.plate_color: Yellow with black characters is common; also white and blue plates. Text is in Lao script and numerals.
vehicles.plate_format: Not confirmed — verify format and any province coding against sources.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: More pickups and older vehicles than Vietnam; not the same scooter swarm. Increasingly Chinese-brand vehicles.

google_coverage.coverage_notes: Limited — Vientiane plus the main highways and a scattering of towns, with large gaps. Outside the capital the Google car is often visible in shot.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Lao and Thai scripts look similar at a glance; both are Theravada Buddhist, both have black-and-white angular bollards and Mekong lowland scenery
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Laos drives on the RIGHT, Thailand on the LEFT — the fastest tell. Laos is far poorer and more mountainous, with sparser, lower-quality coverage, more dirt roads, and the rounder, simpler Lao script.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Mountainous, forested, Buddhist, right-hand traffic, rice paddies
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Vietnamese is heavily-accented Latin script; Lao is its own abugida. Vietnam is much more developed and densely built, with motorbike swarms and tube houses.

confusion_set.shared_traits: South-East Asian Buddhist context, French colonial traces, right-hand traffic, patchy coverage
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Khmer script is angular and dense, unlike rounded Lao. Cambodia is flat; Laos is mountainous with the Mekong hemmed by hills.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Buddhist South-East Asia, right-hand traffic, mountainous, limited coverage
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Burmese script is made of circles and is unmistakable next to Lao. Myanmar's cars are a chaotic mix of left- and right-hand-drive on right-hand roads.
